description: Stiff fingers in the morning are usually a glide problem, not a strength problem. Count your full fists in thirty seconds, learn how finger tendons slide through their tunnels and why movement is their medicine, and get the daily glide routine that frees them up.

scenes.narration: Hold one hand up, fingers spread wide and straight, every joint fully open. Now close it into the tightest fist you own, fingertips pressing into the palm, thumb wrapped over. Open again, completely. That full swing, open to closed to open, is one rep. Start a thirty second clock and count how many complete swings your hand can make without cheating the ends. A fist that stops short of the palm does not count, and fingers that will not fully straighten do not count either, because the test is not speed, it is travel. Try the other hand too. Most people discover one hand is noticeably slower and stickier, usually the one that has been stiff in the mornings. That count is your glide number. Keep it. At the end, I will tell you what it means.

scenes.label: FULL FISTS IN THIRTY SECONDS
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twenty full fists in thirty seconds is where a hand stops feeling like a rusty hinge and starts feeling like a tool again. Under twelve, the glide is sticky: your finger tendons are not traveling their full distance, and the hand compensates with effort that feels like weakness but is actually friction. Between twelve and twenty, the travel is returning and the mornings should already be easing. Over twenty six, your cables run like silk, the kind of glide climbers and guitarists depend on without knowing it exists. Take this test in the morning for the honest grade, because a stiff hand at seven in the evening has been warmed by a whole day of free practice.
scenes.sub: under 12: the glide is sticky - over 26: silk cables

scenes.narration: Look at what a fist actually requires. Your finger muscles live in your forearm, and their force reaches your fingers through long tendons that slide back and forth inside tight tunnels of tissue called sheaths and pulleys. One full fist needs those tendons to travel a surprising distance, centimeters of glide, pulled through the tunnels like cables through conduit. When the glide is free, the fist is effortless. When the tunnel is swollen, dry, or simply unpracticed, the cable drags, and the hand feels stiff, slow, and strangely weak even though the muscles pulling it are perfectly strong. That is the entire point of this episode's title. Finger healing matters more than finger muscle because there is barely any muscle in a finger. There is only cable and tunnel, and the relationship between them is called glide. Restore the glide and the strength you already have suddenly arrives at the fingertips.

Now why mornings are the worst, and why that pattern is good news. Tendons are not fed the way muscles are. Their blood supply is thin, so they take in much of their nutrition by diffusion, soaking up fluid from their surroundings, and that soaking is pumped by movement itself. Glide the tendon and fluid exchanges. Rest it all night and the tunnels sit in stale fluid, slightly swollen, slightly sticky, which is why the first fists of the day feel like opening a rusty gate and the tenth feels almost normal. Stiffness that melts within minutes of moving is the signature of a glide and fluid problem, and it is one of the most fixable patterns in this whole season. Stiffness that never melts is a different story, and we will cover that rule at the end. For the melting kind, the prescription is embarrassingly simple: move the cables, early, often, through their full travel, and let the pump do its work.

Hand therapists have a classic sequence for exactly this, and it is worth stealing. The fingers move through three positions: fully straight, then a hook, bending only the middle joints with the fingertips reaching toward the base of the fingers, then a full fist. Each position slides the two finger tendons by different amounts relative to each other and to their tunnels, so the full sequence scrubs the whole travel path instead of just the easy middle of it. Done slowly, with a pause in each position, it is less like exercise and more like flossing for tendons: unglamorous, slightly tedious, and quietly the difference between cables that drag and cables that glide. This is also why random squeezing is not enough. A squeeze ball trains the close. The sequence trains the journey, and stiffness lives on the journey.

lines: its glide a hundred times daily.
beats.title: THE CHEAP REPS

beats.text: KEYBOARDS COUNT IF YOU TRAVEL FULLY

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage in your hands. Your fingers are light, the distances are short, and the load of a glide session is essentially zero, which means you can practice at a frequency no other joint in this season allows: at your desk, in the shower, on a walk, a hundred full travels a day without a single minute of formal exercise. Bigger, thicker hands fight more tissue drag and more swelling with every attempt. Yours can sneak the reps in under the day's radar, and glide responds to exactly that: many easy travels, never forced, never far apart. The hand that types and games all day is not doomed to stiffness. It is one honest routine away from being the most practiced hand in the room.

Train with me. Straight hand, hook, full fist, holding each position for a breath, slow enough to feel the cables travel. Forty seconds of gliding, twenty of rest, three rounds. Both hands, even if only one complains.

beats.text: GLIDES BEFORE YOUR FEET SWING OUT
TRACK THE MELT, NOT THE PAIN

scenes.narration: Here is your routine. First thing in the morning, before your feet swing out of bed, run the glide sequence ten times on each hand and time how long the stiffness takes to melt. That melt time is your progress meter, and it should shrink week by week. Through the day, repeat the sequence whenever your hands have been still for an hour, and use warm water as an amplifier whenever you can: glides in a warm shower are the deluxe version. The mistakes to retire: forcing a stuck finger straight or bent to prove it can, retired, tunnels hate violence. Cracking your knuckles as your entire mobility plan, retired. Splinting stiff fingers still all day, retired, stillness is the disease here, not the cure. And the rule: if one finger starts locking or catching with a snap, if a single joint swells and stays swollen, or if stiffness follows an injury and never melts at all, see a professional if it persists. Catching fingers and single hot joints are specific diagnoses with specific fixes.

So, your count. Under twelve full fists: your cables are dragging, and the morning routine was designed for exactly this reading. Twelve to twenty: the travel is coming back, keep the glides frequent and watch the melt time shrink. Over twenty: your hands glide like tools again, and a minute of glides a day is all the maintenance they ask. Comment your count and your melt time, because the melt is the number nobody else is tracking and it tells the truth first. In thirty days we count fists again, first thing in the morning, no warm-up, honest rules. Fingers do not heal by getting stronger. They heal by getting their glide back, and glide is just movement, repeated kindly.

Your hands open and close ten thousand times a day. They deserve cables that travel freely. Glide them every morning, and in thirty days we count together. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Why Your finger tendon healing Matter More Than Muscle (The finger stiffness Episode)
